title: OpenAI Eavesdropping Case Suspect Granted Bail: $1 Million Bond + Electronic Ankle Monitor; Judge Says Evidence Insufficient to Continue Detention

content_html:
A case triggered by a “listening device wrapped in toilet paper” in an executive conference room has taken a turn. On November 24 local time, the U.S. federal court in San Francisco ruled that former engineer Al-Fozan, suspected of planting a listening device at OpenAI, may be released on $1 million bail, on the condition that he wear an electronic ankle monitor and remain under home detention.

Judge Relents: Don’t Make This About Nationality

Federal Magistrate Judge Alex Tse, who presided over the hearing, found that the evidence was insufficient to keep him detained pending trial, and that there was no adequate basis to conclude he posed a serious flight risk. He is 35, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident. He was arrested on October 9, indicted by a grand jury on October 27 on a federal charge of unlawful interception of oral communications, and pleaded not guilty on November 6. Prosecutors had opposed release, citing his financial resources and close ties to Saudi Arabia, and also mentioned that before his arrest he held a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia; but the judge held that Saudi ties alone were not enough to establish intent to flee. The defense countered that there was no new evidence supporting claims of trade secret theft, nor any proof of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

A Recorder Wrapped in Toilet Paper

The Department of Justice disclosed that on September 30, OpenAI employees found a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, wrapped in toilet paper. Prosecutors allege that he entered the conference room multiple times to secretly record conversations involving nonpublic information such as R&D, product planning, business partnerships, and strategic decisions. However, the only formal charge is unlawful interception of oral communications; trade secret theft and economic espionage were not included.

The release arrangements have been set: he is expected to leave Santa Clara County Jail on November 25 and return to his residence in Millbrae, California, for home detention, comply with a curfew, not leave the jurisdiction of the Northern District of California, and not contact OpenAI employees or access related materials (except litigation evidence). Of the $1 million bond, he himself is responsible for $500,000, with the remainder guaranteed by three close friends. The trial is scheduled for January 20, 2027.
